What is Deep Learning?

ARTIFICIAL
INTELLIGENCE

MACHINE LEARNING

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Nested fields: AI is the goal, ML is learning from data, DL is ML with neural networks. Key phrase: learn the task directly from raw data, with no hand-written rules or features.

Why Deep Learning?

Manually engineered features are time consuming and not scalable in practice.

Can we learn the underlying features directly from data?

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Old pipeline: humans design features (edge detectors, color histograms). Deep learning learns them, layer by layer: edges, then parts, then whole faces. Ask: how long would it take you to hand-code a 'nose detector'?

Why now?

Neural Networks are decades old...
  • 1982: John Hopfield introduces the Hopfield Network, a recurrent neural network that serves as associative memory, providing a new way to understand how memories can be stored and retrieved in neural systems.
  • 1949: neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch and mathematician Walter Pitts wrote “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity” on how neurons might work
  • 1986: Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams develop backpropagation, making the training of multi-layered neural networks feasible.
  • In 1990, computer scientist Yann André LeCun implemented Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) in their paper “Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition”
  • In 1997, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) was developed by Sepp Hochreiter
  • 2006: Fei-Fei Li begins creating ImageNet, a massive labeled visual dataset to advance machine learning.
  • 2012: AlexNet, created by Alex Krizhevsky and co-supervised by Geoffrey Hinton, wins the ImageNet Challenge, demonstrating the power of deep learning.
  • 2015: Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, and others co-found OpenAI to promote safe and open AI development.
  • 2017: Google researchers introduce the Transformer architecture with the paper “Attention is All You Need,” revolutionizing NLP and leading to models like BERT and GPT.
  • 2022: OpenAI launches ChatGPT, bringing generative AI into the mainstream and demonstrating AI's ability to carry on human-like conversations.
  • 2023: Meta launches LLaMA (Large Language Model Meta AI), aiming to democratize access to powerful language models.
  • 2024: Geoffrey Hinton and John Hopfield receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for their foundational work in machine learning with artificial neural networks.

Why the resurgence?

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Walk the timeline quickly. The core ideas (neuron 1943, SGD 1952, perceptron 1958, backprop 1986, CNN 1990) are old. Click to show the 2024 Nobel Prize: the field is now recognized as fundamental science.

Why now?

“If Deep Learning is the steam engine of the AI revolution, then data is its coal: the raw material that powers our intelligent machines, without which nothing would be possible”

Big Data

  • Larger datasets
  • Easier collection and storage
    • The rise of the internet make it feasible to collect and distribute very large datasets
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
First reason for the resurgence: data. ImageNet has over 14 million labeled images; the internet made collecting data cheap.

Why now?

Hardware

  • gaming market subsidized supercomputing for the next generation of artificial intelligence applications
  • Massively parallel chips
  • Graphics Processing Units (GPUs)
  • In 2016, Google revealed its Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) project: a new chip design developed from the ground up to run deep neural networks significantly faster and far more energy efficient than top-of-the-line GPUs
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Second reason: hardware. Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplication, which GPUs (built for games) do in parallel. TPUs are chips designed only for this.

Why now?

Software

  • Algorithms
    • advent of several simple but important algorithmic improvements that allowed for better gradient propagation:
      • activation functions for neural layers
      • weight initialization schemes
      • optimization schemes
  • Toolboxes
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Third reason: software. Better activations, initialization and optimizers, plus free toolboxes (Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch) that compute gradients automatically. We use TensorFlow in today's demo.

Discussion

Why did deep learning take off only recently?

  1. Backpropagation was published in 1986, yet deep learning took off around 2012. What changed in between?

    Large labeled datasets such as ImageNet, GPUs that made training fast enough, and better tricks (ReLU, initialization, optimizers). The algorithms were old; the fuel and the engine were new.

  2. Think of an app you used today. Where do you think the training data came from?

    Usually from the users themselves: clicks, photos, typed text, ratings. This is the “data is the coal” idea.

  3. Name a task where hand-crafted rules might still beat a learned model.

    Small, well-understood problems with little data or strict rules, such as tax computation or a grading rubric. Learning pays off when patterns are too complex to write down.

Artificial Neural Network

Common Activation Functions

Activation Function

  • Non-linear
    • model patterns in dataset are non-linear
  • Continuously differentiable
    • to improve model using gradient descent, output must have a nice slope so error derivatives with respect to weights can be computed
  • Fixed Range
    • squash the input data into a narrow range that keeps outputs bounded and training stable (e.g. 0 to 1 for sigmoid, −1 to 1 for tanh)
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Three properties we want: non-linear, differentiable (for gradient descent) and often a bounded range. Briefly point at the table; the next slide compares the three you'll use most.

Artificial Neural Network

Sigmoid, Tanh and ReLU

The three activation functions you will meet most often, and their slopes (what gradient descent uses).

Sigmoid

  • Output between 0 and 1, so it reads as a probability
  • Used in the output layer for yes/no problems
  • Slope is at most 0.25 and near 0 for large |z|, so gradients shrink in deep networks

Hyperbolic tangent

  • Output between −1 and 1, centered at 0
  • Steeper than sigmoid (slope up to 1)
  • Still flattens out for large |z|

ReLU

  • Cheap to compute
  • Slope stays 1 for positive inputs, so deep networks train faster
  • The usual default for hidden layers
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Sigmoid for yes/no outputs, tanh is zero-centered, ReLU is the default for hidden layers. Point at the slopes: sigmoid's maximum slope is 0.25, which matters later for backprop.

Artificial Neural Network

Importance of Activation Functions

The purpose of activation functions is to introduce non-linearities into the network.

Without an activation function, the output will always be linear.

Non-linearities allows us to approximate arbitrarily complex functions.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
The data is not linearly separable. Click: a straight line cannot do it, no matter how we place it.

Artificial Neural Network

Importance of Activation Functions

Linear activations produce linear decisions no matter the network size

Non-linearities allow us to approximate arbitrarily complex functions

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Without activations, stacking layers still gives a straight line. With non-linearities the network can bend the boundary around the data.

Discussion

Check your understanding: building networks

  1. How many weights and biases does a network with 2 inputs, 3 hidden units and 1 output have?

    Hidden layer: 2×3 + 3 = 9. Output layer: 3×1 + 1 = 4. Total 13 trainable parameters.

  2. If we remove every activation function, what does a 10-layer network compute?

    Still just a linear function of the inputs. A product of linear maps is linear, so depth adds nothing without non-linearities.

  3. What do we gain by adding more layers, and what does it cost?

    More layers can learn more complex features (edges → parts → faces). They need more data, more computation, and are harder to train.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Discussion: parameter counting and why depth needs non-linearity. Answer for the first question: 13.

Quantifying Loss

The loss of our network measures the cost incurred from incorrect predictions

Predicted: 0.1
Actual: 1.0
PredictedActual
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
The loss turns 'how wrong' into a number. Purple is the prediction, blue is the true label.

Empirical Loss

The empirical loss measures the total loss over entire dataset

f(x)y
0.10.80.6⋮
✗✗✓

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Average the loss over every student in the dataset: this is the empirical loss J(W), what training minimizes.

Mean Squared Error Loss

Mean squared error loss can be used with regression models that output continuous real numbers

f(x)y
308085⋮
✗✗✓ 
902095⋮
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
For numeric outputs (like a grade), use mean squared error: square the differences, then average.

Binary Cross-Entropy Loss

Cross-entropy loss can be used with models that output a probability between 0 and 1

Back to our student: Predicted: 0.1 · Actual: 1.0

Squared error: (1.0 - 0.1)² = 0.81 Cross-entropy: -log(0.1) = 2.30

A confident wrong answer costs much more with cross-entropy, so the model gets a stronger push to fix it.

  • Use mean squared error for regression (predicting a number such as a grade)
  • Use binary cross-entropy for yes/no classification (pass or fail), with a sigmoid output
  • In Keras: loss="mse" or loss="binary_crossentropy"
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
For pass/fail, cross-entropy is the better choice. Compare the numbers: 0.81 for squared error vs 2.30 for cross-entropy on the same mistake.

Example Problem in TensorFlow: Will I pass this class?

import tensorflow as tf model = tf.keras.Sequential([ tf.keras.Input(shape=(2,)), # x1 = activities, x2 = hours tf.keras.layers.Dense(3, activation="sigmoid"), # z1, z2, z3 tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"), # y-hat ]) model.compile( optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.1), loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"]) model.fit(X, y, epochs=200, batch_size=8) # gradient descent model.predict([[4, 5]]) # our new student
  • Dense(3) has 2×3 weights + 3 biases = 9 parameters
  • Dense(1) has 3×1 weights + 1 bias = 4 parameters
  • compile picks the loss and the optimizer; fit runs forward propagation, backpropagation and the weight updates for us
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
The whole example in about ten lines of Keras. compile chooses loss and optimizer; fit runs forward pass, backprop and updates. We will run this in the demo.

Discussion

Discussion: choosing a loss

  1. Which loss would you use to predict a student’s final grade (0–100)? To predict pass or fail?

    Grade: mean squared error (regression). Pass/fail: binary cross-entropy with a sigmoid output (classification).

  2. Why should a confident wrong answer (predict 0.01, actual 1) cost more than an unsure one (predict 0.4)?

    We want the model to be calibrated: overconfident mistakes are the most harmful, and cross-entropy (−log 0.01 ≈ 4.6 vs −log 0.4 ≈ 0.9) punishes them hardest.

  3. If every student in our training data passed, what would the model learn?

    To always predict “pass”. The loss would be low, but the model would be useless. Data quality and balance matter as much as the model.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Discussion on choosing losses and the importance of balanced data.

Training Neural Networks

Section: how do we find good weights?

Loss Optimization

We want to find network weights that achieve the lowest loss

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Frame training as a search problem. Every possible setting of the weights gives a different loss. Picture all those settings as a landscape: position = the weights, height = the loss J(W). Training means finding the lowest point. Why not just try every setting? Even our tiny 13-parameter network has infinitely many combinations, and real networks have millions or billions of weights. Brute force is impossible, so we need a smarter way to search. Click to show the surface. Point out: there are hills (bad weights), valleys (good weights) and more than one valley (local minima). Ask: "If you were dropped somewhere on this surface blindfolded, how would you find the bottom?"

Gradient Descent

The optimization technique that powers modern neural networks.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
The hiker in the fog. You are on a mountain in thick fog and want to reach the valley. You can't see the bottom, but you can feel the slope under your feet. So you take a step in the direction that goes downhill most steeply, feel again, step again. Eventually you reach low ground. Map the analogy carefully: • Your position = the current weights • Your altitude = the loss • The slope you feel under your feet = the gradient • The size of each step = the learning rate Two key points: 1. We only use local information. The algorithm never sees the whole landscape, only the slope where it currently stands, which is cheap to compute. 2. The black path on the surface shows this. Two different starting points can end in two different valleys. That is why initialization matters, and why we may not find the global minimum (in practice a good valley is usually enough).

Gradient Descent

Consider a continuous function that maps a number x to a new number y

A small change in x can only result in a small change in y

Increase x by a small factor epsilon_x this results in a small epsilon_y change to y

When epsilon_x is small enough around a certain point p, it is possible to approximate f as a linear function of a slope a, so that

f(x + epsilon_x) = y + a * epsilon_x

The slope a is called the derivative of f in p.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Build the 'feel the slope' idea in one dimension first. The derivative answers: "If I nudge x a tiny bit, how much does y change?" Walk through the picture: move x right by a small epsilon_x and y changes by epsilon_y. Close enough to a point, the curve looks like a straight line, and its slope a = epsilon_y / epsilon_x is the derivative. Everyday version: speed is the derivative of distance. A slope of 3 means "for every small step right, the output goes up about 3 times as much." This local straight-line view is the whole trick: we can't see the full curve, but near where we stand it behaves like a line, and lines are easy to reason about.

Gradient Descent

The slope a is called the derivative of f in p.

f(x + epsilon_x) = y + a * epsilon_x

a < 0 means a small increase in x around p will result in in a decrease of f(x)

a > 0 means a small increase in x around p will result in an increase of f(x)

The absolute value of a, the magnitude of the derivative, will tell you how quickly the decrease/increase will happen

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Turn the derivative into a decision rule. • Slope negative (a < 0): moving right goes downhill, so increase x. • Slope positive (a > 0): moving right goes uphill, so decrease x. • Either way: move in the direction opposite to the sign of the slope. That is why the update has a minus sign. The magnitude |a| tells us how steep it is. Far from the minimum the slope is steep and the steps are naturally big; near the minimum the slope flattens and steps shrink on their own. At the bottom the slope is 0, so the updates stop. This is why gradient descent slows down and settles as it converges. Quick check: draw a U-shaped curve on the board, put a dot on the left side, and ask which way to move and why (slope negative, so move right).

Gradient Descent

Algorithm

  1. Initialize weights randomly or with zeros
  2. Loop until convergence:
    1. Compute the gradient of the loss function with respect to the parameters (weights)
    2. Update the weights by moving them a small step in the opposite direction of the gradient (gradient always points to the direction where the function increases the fastest)
  3. Return the final weights when convergence criteria are met (e.g. decrease in loss, reaching maximum number of iterations)
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Read the algorithm as the hiker's routine: look at the slope, take a step against it, repeat. Note on step 2b: the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, so we go the opposite way, steepest decrease. When do we stop? In practice: after a fixed number of steps (epochs), or when the loss stops improving, or when it starts getting worse on validation data. Ask: "Why initialize randomly rather than all zeros?" (In a network, identical weights produce identical hidden units that get identical updates, so they never become different. Random starts break that symmetry.)

Gradient Descent

A gradient is a vector of partial derivatives of a multivariable function, indicating the direction and rate of the steepest increase in the function’s value.

The partial derivative of a function with respect to a variable is the derivative assuming all other input variables are held constant.

Given the following cost function:

Translated as a linear function,

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
From one dimension to many. With two or more parameters, the slope becomes a gradient: one partial derivative per parameter. Each partial derivative asks the 1-D question for one weight while all the others are frozen: "If I nudge only m, how does the loss change?" Analogy: you are standing on the hillside. Facing east, the ground slopes one way; facing north, another. The gradient combines both into one arrow pointing straight uphill. We step along the opposite arrow. Connect to the formula: J(W) from the loss slides becomes f(m, b) when our model is a straight line y = mx + b. So m and b are our 'weights' here.

Gradient Descent

The gradient can be calculated as,

We iterate through our data points using our new and values and compute the partial derivatives. This new gradient tells us the slope of our cost function at our current position (current parameter values) and the direction we should move to update our parameters.

The resulting gradient is a vector with one value for each parameter

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Interpret each component; don't just derive it. The common factor (y_i − (m x_i + b)) is the error on point i. • ∂f/∂b sums the errors. If the line is mostly too low (positive errors), the derivative is negative, so b goes up. The line shifts toward the data. • ∂f/∂m weights each error by x_i. Points far from the origin have more say in the slope, which makes sense because changing m moves those points the most. So the gradient is a summary of the mistakes: which direction, and how much each parameter is to blame. Every iteration recomputes it at the new position, because the landscape's slope changes as we move. The notebook (section 4) shows this loop running on a simple curve.

Gradient Descent by Hand: Hours Studied vs Quiz Score

Three students: (1 h, 2 pts), (2 h, 4 pts), (3 h, 6 pts). Model . Start at , learning rate .

predictions ŷ = 0, 0, 0 errors y − ŷ = 2, 4, 6 loss = (2² + 4² + 6²) / 3 = 56 / 3 = 18.67
df/dm = (1/3) Σ −2 · x · error = −2/3 · (1·2 + 2·4 + 3·6) = −2/3 · 28 = −18.67 df/db = (1/3) Σ −2 · error = −2/3 · (2 + 4 + 6) = −2/3 · 12 = −8.00

Both slopes are negative: increasing m or b lowers the loss, so the update will increase them.

m = 0 − 0.1 · (−18.67) = 1.87 b = 0 − 0.1 · (−8.00) = 0.80 new loss = 0.30 (was 18.67)

Blue dots: the data · grey: start (m = 0, b = 0) · red: after step 1

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
A concrete, calculator-friendly example. Three students; the true pattern is score = 2 × hours, so the best answer is m = 2, b = 0. Students should not know this yet; ask them to guess the line first. Click 1: with m = b = 0 the line predicts 0 for everyone, so the errors are 2, 4, 6 and the loss (mean squared error) is 18.67. Click 2: plug into the gradient formulas from the previous slide. Point out the x inside df/dm: the student who studied 3 hours contributes the most to the slope gradient, because changing m moves that prediction the most. Both gradients are negative: "uphill" is toward smaller m and b, so we go the other way. Click 3: one step of size 0.1 gives m = 1.87, b = 0.80, and the loss drops from 18.67 to 0.30. Have students verify one prediction: 1.87 × 3 + 0.80 = 6.40 vs actual 6. Ask: why didn't we land exactly on m = 2, b = 0? (The gradient only tells us the direction and steepness where we stand, not where the bottom is.)

Target: m = 2, b = 0 (score = 2 × hours). Same numbers in notebook section 4.

grey: step 0 · yellow: step 1 · green: step 10 · red: step 200

  • Big drop first: the loss falls from 18.7 to 0.3 in one step, because the slope is steep far from the minimum.
  • Overshoot: at step 2, m goes down (1.87 → 1.67). Step 1 overshot, so the gradient changed sign.
  • Slow finish: near the bottom the slope is almost flat, so steps get tiny.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Same problem, run for 200 steps. Walk down the table with the class. Three things to notice, all from the intuition slides: 1. The biggest improvement happens immediately (18.67 → 0.30). Far from the minimum the slope is steep, so the step is large. 2. m overshoots: 1.87 at step 1, then down to 1.67 at step 2. After step 1 the gradient for m became positive (+1.96), so the next update reversed direction. This is the zig-zag from the learning-rate slides on a small scale. 3. The finish is slow: from step 10 to step 200 we only move from 1.75 to 2.00. Near the bottom the slope is nearly zero, so each step is tiny. That's why training runs for many epochs, and why stopping criteria matter. Ask: what would happen with η = 0.5? (Try it in the notebook: it overshoots wildly and diverges.) And with η = 0.01? (Smooth but needs about 10× more steps.)

Gradient Descent in the Real World

The same three steps everywhere: measure the error, find which way each weight should move, take a small step.

Adjusting the shower

Too cold (the error)? Turn the knob toward hot, by an amount that matches how cold it is. Turn it too far at once and you get scalded, then freezing: a learning rate that is too big.

Predicting house prices

Weights for floor area, location, age. If the model keeps under-pricing large houses, the gradient for the floor-area weight is negative, so that weight goes up a little after each batch.

Spam filter

Each word has a weight. An email with “free prize” was marked safe but was spam: the gradient raises the weights of “free” and “prize” so similar emails score as spam next time.

Recommendations (YouTube, Netflix, Spotify)

The loss compares predicted with actual watch time or skips. Mini-batches of user activity nudge millions of weights so recommendations match what you actually watch.

Large language models

Billions of weights, trained to predict the next word. The update rule is the same , repeated over trillions of words on thousands of GPUs.

Your grades

After each quiz (the loss) you look at what went wrong (the gradient) and adjust how you study. Small, regular adjustments beat changing everything at once.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Use these to make the abstract loop concrete. Pick two or three rather than reading all six. The shower is the best everyday analogy: the feedback (temperature) tells you the direction and roughly how much, and an over-eager hand on the knob is a learning rate that's too large. Ask students if they have overshot a shower before; most have. House prices and spam are classic ML examples where you can name the weights. Emphasize that the model doesn't know any rules about houses or spam; it only follows the gradient of its loss. Recommendations and LLMs show the scale: the same subtraction from slide 49 runs billions of times. The only differences are size, mini-batches and optimizers that adapt the step size (such as Adam). Close with the grades analogy and the discussion question: "What is your loss function when you study, and what is your learning rate?"

Gradient Descent: The Update Rule

Every weight takes a small step against its gradient. is the learning rate.

# gradient descent, written out W = random_init() while not converged: grad = dJ_dW(W) # backpropagation W = W - lr * grad # update return W

The same step in TensorFlow:

with tf.GradientTape() as tape: loss = loss_fn(y, model(X)) # forward pass grads = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables) optimizer.apply_gradients( zip(grads, model.trainable_variables))

Next we do this by hand for one small network, one weight at a time.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
This is the one equation to remember from today: new weight = old weight − learning rate × slope. Go through it piece by piece: • ∂J/∂W: which direction is uphill, and how steep • the minus sign: go downhill instead • η (eta, the learning rate): how big a step to take Every modern optimizer (SGD, momentum, Adam) is a variation on this one line. The differences are in how the step is computed. Show the TensorFlow version: GradientTape records the forward pass, tape.gradient computes ∂J/∂W for every weight (this is backpropagation, done for us), and apply_gradients performs the subtraction. Transition: "TensorFlow computes these gradients automatically. To understand what it is doing, we'll compute them by hand once."

Backward Propagation

2 comes from the power rule of differentiation. When you differentiate (actual-predicted)² with respect to predicted the exponent decreases by 1.

-1 comes from chain rule when taking the derivative of E with respect to predicted.

The chain rule requires you to multiply the derivative of the outer function E by the derivative of the inner function (actual - predicted) with respect to predicted. The derivative of -predicted with respect to predicted is -1
When we take the partial derivative of the total error E with respect o1 the quantity ½(actualo2 - predictedo2)² becomes 0 because o1 does not affect it.

It means we are taking the derivative of a constant which is 0.

Learning Rate

Recall that we update the weights so we can move the weights by “a bit” in a direction that will reduce the loss. The magnitude of the move is determined by a small quantity called learning rate.

Learning rate is the size of the steps we take towards a local minimum.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
The learning rate is the length of the hiker's stride. Two parabolas with the same starting point: • η = 0.1: small, careful steps that steadily approach the minimum. • η = 0.8: steps so large they jump across the valley to the other side. Here it still gets closer each time, but it zig-zags. Why does a too-large step overshoot? The gradient is only accurate locally (the 'straight line near the point' idea from earlier). A big step goes beyond the region where that approximation holds, so the step lands somewhere the slope is very different. Analogy: walking down stairs. Tiny steps are slow but safe; leaping several stairs at once may land you past the landing.

Learning Rate

  • If learning rate is too small, Gradient Descent takes longer to converge or may even reach maximum iteration before reaching an optimal point
  • If learning rate is too big, Gradient descent may not converge to an optimal point, overshoot, or diverge completely.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
This curve has a flat shoulder near x = 0 and a deeper valley at x ≈ 1.5. • Too small: progress stalls on the flat shoulder because the slope (and so the step) is tiny there. It may hit the iteration limit before reaching the valley. • Too big: it overshoots the valley, oscillates, or diverges (the loss grows without bound). • Just right: reaches the valley in a reasonable number of steps. Practical advice for students: • Start with a standard value (0.01 for SGD, 0.001 for Adam). • Plot the loss curve. Flat and slowly decreasing means raise the learning rate; jumpy or increasing means lower it. • Notebook section 5 compares 0.01, 0.5 and 20 on the same model.

Batch, Stochastic and Mini-batch Gradient Descent

How many examples do we use to compute each gradient?

Batch

  • Uses the whole dataset per step
  • Accurate gradient, smooth path
  • Slow and memory-hungry on big data

Stochastic (SGD)

  • One random example per step
  • Very fast steps, noisy path
  • The 1952 idea on our timeline

Mini-batch

  • A small batch (e.g. B = 32) per step
  • Good balance of speed and stability
  • Fits GPU parallelism; what we use in practice
model.fit(X, y, epochs=50, batch_size=32) # one epoch = one pass over all n examples
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Back to the hiker: computing the exact gradient means surveying the whole mountain (every training example) before each step. With a million examples that is very slow. • Batch: survey everything, then take one precise step. • Stochastic (SGD): look at one random example and step immediately. Each step is a noisy guess at downhill, but you take many more steps per second. On average the noise cancels out, and it can even help shake the model out of shallow valleys. • Mini-batch: look at a small group (say 32) and step. This is the practical compromise: much less noisy than SGD, much faster than full batch, and it uses GPU parallelism well. Analogy: estimating class opinion. Asking everyone is accurate but slow; asking one random person is fast but unreliable; asking a random group of 32 is a good balance. Vocabulary: an epoch is one full pass through the training data. With 150 students and batch_size 16 that's about 10 update steps per epoch.

Discussion

Discussion: training

  1. In the worked example, went from 0.40 to 0.3755. Why did it go down?

    Its gradient was positive (+0.0816): increasing would raise , but is already too high (0.7569 vs 0.01). So we step the other way.

  2. Why did change much less (0.15 → 0.1499) than ?

    Its gradient is a product of more small factors: a sigmoid slope (≤ 0.25) and a small input (). In deep networks this shrinking is called the vanishing gradient problem, one reason ReLU is popular.

  3. What might happen if we used a learning rate of 5 instead of 0.3?

    The steps could overshoot the minimum and the loss could bounce or blow up (diverge). Too small and training crawls.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Discussion: why w5 moved down, and why w1 barely moved (vanishing gradients).

Cost Functions in Neural Networks

Section: the role of cost functions.

Understanding How Models Measure and Minimize Errors

A cost (or loss) function acts as a guide for how the model learns

Helps the model
measure how wrong its predictions are and
adjust its internal parameters to improve over time.

  • Each prediction made by the model is compared to the true label or value
  • The cost function computes a numerical score that represents the difference between them
  • The goal of training is to minimize the loss / cost
  • Lower lost / Lower cost means better performance
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Three roles: measure error, compare predictions with true values, and give training a target to minimize. Click through the three panels.

Why Cost Functions Matter

Cost Function

  • Measures performance
    • a single number that tells us how far the predictions are from the true values
  • Guides optimization
    • gradient descent uses the derivative of the cost with respect to each weight to decide how to update it
  • Matches the task
    • mean squared error for regression models that output continuous real numbers; cross-entropy is commonly used for classification
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Why the choice matters: the cost function defines what 'good' means for the model.

Discussion

Wrap-up discussion

  1. Is a lower training loss always better?

    Not always. A model can memorize the training data and fail on new students (overfitting). We check performance on data the model has never seen.

  2. Our model uses only activities passed and hours on the project. What other features could help?

    Attendance, quiz scores, submission timeliness. Better features often help more than a bigger network.

  3. Where in your own field or hobby could a small neural network help?

    Open discussion. Ask: what are the inputs, what is the output, which loss fits, and where would the data come from?

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Wrap-up discussion: overfitting preview and feature ideas.

Summary

  1. A perceptron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, then applies a non-linear activation: .
  2. Stacking perceptrons into layers gives a neural network; non-linearities let it learn complex decision boundaries.
  3. A loss function scores how wrong the predictions are: mean squared error for numbers, cross-entropy for classes.
  4. Gradient descent lowers the loss by moving each weight against its gradient, scaled by the learning rate.
  5. Backpropagation uses the chain rule to get every gradient, from the output layer back to the first layer.
  6. In practice we train on mini-batches, and frameworks such as TensorFlow compute the gradients for us.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Lecture 01
Six key points to remember. Ask a student to explain backprop in one sentence.
